newsitem.title: GERMANY: Vebacom, Colt set to win German phone licences.
newsitem.headline: Vebacom, Colt set to win German phone licences.

text.p: Germany could issue its first three licences for public telecommunications services on Thursday, paving the way for competition to Deutsche Telekom in basic phone services in 1998, industry sources said on Wednesday.

The award kicks off the last stage of preparation as companies gear up their networks and begin honing strategies they hope will convince Germans to drop Telekom in favour of new competitors entering the market.

Setting the stage for the "big bang", when deregulation sweeps through European telecoms on January 1, 1998, Britain's Colt Telecom, Vebacom GmbH, and NetCologne have been picked to receive the government's first public phone licences.
"Colt will be among the first three companies to be awarded a licence," said Angelika Scheiffele, marketing manager for Colt's Frankfurt-based German operations.
"We applied for a licence covering Frankfurt, Berlin, Hamburg and Munich and we have been informed it will be approved," she added.

Industry sources said that in addition to Colt, the government had also approved licences for Vebacom, the joint venture between energy group Veba AG and Cable and Wireless, and NetCologne, a local operator.
"We presume that we will get our licence this year," said a spokeswoman for Vebacom. "But we have not heard anything definitive yet."
NetCologne, which wants to offer basic phone services in the greater Cologne region, declined to comment. Of the three licences, only Vebacom's will be for nation-wide service.

The so-called "class four" licences cover basic voice telephone services for the public. That is the only service still under monopoly protection in Germany, where the telecoms market is expected to be worth more than 100 billion marks ($64.5 billion) by the year 2000.
The Post and Telecommunications Ministry confirmed that it would make an announcement about the licences this week, but would not say which companies would receive licences.
"I can say definitively that no licence has been awarded today," a spokesman said.
Post and Telecommunications Minister Wolfgang Boetsch told reporters late on Tuesday there were currently 11 applications for licences to provide public telephone services pending.
Seven of the applications are for a national telephone service and the rest are for regional service.
"The licences could be awarded this week," a spokesman for the minister told Reuters.

Next year will see some of the world's largest players on the telecommunications market and their German partners, several of Germany's biggest enterprises, make their final moves to compete against monopoly Telekom beginning in 1998.

A dispute over the costs of the licences has been simmering for months. The government, seeking to plug yawning budget deficits, hopes to gain around 1.6 billion marks in one-off fees for new telecommunications licences.
At around 40 million marks for a nation-wide licence, industry representatives have called this an "investment tax" that would become just another excuse not to invest in Germany.
"I don't see any barriers to entering the market," he said.
